vignette:
At 46, Minh had been living for years with a version of himself that felt perpetually braced. He was a married Vietnamese American software engineer, quiet and meticulous at work, the kind of man colleagues trusted to solve complicated problems without much fuss. Before seeking help, he had tried to keep his inner life partitioned off from the rest of his day, but the partition had become harder to maintain. The war zone he had once moved through in uniform no longer stayed in the past in any stable way. Certain sensations brought it back with an immediacy that made no sense to him and yet felt undeniable.

When Minh spoke about the combat event itself, he stalled, fell silent, and looked down. He said he could not seem to put what happened into words, and this was not reluctance in the ordinary sense so much as a genuine failure of language. When he tried, the account broke apart into sensory fragments. He could describe the smell before anything else: a harsh, unmistakable odor that now, years later, could still seize him if he encountered anything remotely similar. He remembered noise just as vividly. In his mind there was the mechanical sound of engines, and the whole scene would return not as a story with a beginning and end but as a film that played over and over, abrupt and intrusive, as if a clip had been looped somewhere outside his control. In those moments he did not merely think about the event; he sometimes heard in his head the same sounds he had heard during it, as though his memory had its own soundtrack.

The detail that stayed most charged for him was exposure and helplessness. During the event, being physically vulnerable had become fused in his mind with mortal danger. That was why situations involving nakedness now carried so much force. Something as ordinary as stepping out of the shower could produce a flash of alarm before he had fully dried off and dressed. He was not confused about where he was; he knew he was at home. But his body reacted as if being uncovered meant being defenseless, visible, at risk. What frightened him most was the suddenness with which that sense could take over.

Over the months and years afterward, Minh shaped his life around not stirring these reactions up. He stopped watching war films and avoided television programs, articles, or anything else that might resemble combat. If his wife put on a movie and a scene turned military, he would leave the room without explanation or ask to change it. He also began going out less than he used to. At first this looked like tiredness after work, but it gradually became a pattern: errands postponed, social invitations declined, weekends spent almost entirely at home. Exercise dropped away too. He had once tried to maintain a routine, but exertion made him feel too exposed and keyed up, and he came to avoid it altogether.

His home, which he wanted to experience as safe, did not fully feel that way. Minh said he was on guard even inside his own house. He checked locks, listened for sounds outside, and tracked movement near the windows without quite meaning to. In public, strangers approaching him in ordinary situations could feel threatening before he had any reason to judge them that way. A man stepping too close in a checkout line or someone turning toward him on the sidewalk could trigger a rapid internal calculation of distance, intent, escape. Unfamiliar places were especially difficult because he felt he could not assess the danger there. If his wife suggested trying a new restaurant or visiting somewhere outside his usual routes, he often resisted or found a reason not to go. At work, this showed up when his team planned off-site gatherings; Minh preferred to remain in the predictable environment of his office or, increasingly, work from home, where he knew the layout and could monitor who entered his space.

The motorcycle noise was among the most disruptive triggers in his daily life. From his home office, the sudden revving of an engine on the street could make the looping film start again before he had finished the line of code in front of him. For a moment he would hear the remembered sounds layered over the present one, and his concentration would vanish. Related smells could do the same thing outdoors, which made leaving the house feel even less manageable. He had come to believe that ordinary life was full of things he could not reliably scan in advance, and that belief narrowed his world further.

By the time he sought help, the costs were no longer containable within private discomfort. His wife had begun to tell him how small their shared life had become, how often plans were built around what he could avoid. Minh did not come in speaking in psychological terms. He said he was tired of feeling watchful all the time and tired of not being able to explain what had happened even though it was still so present. He was afraid that the memories would keep arriving as the same relentless film, with the same sounds in his head, and that he would go on withdrawing from more and more of life. What he hoped for, cautiously, was simpler: to go outside without scanning everything, to be in his own home without feeling on guard, and to find some way at last to say what happened.
